# Basic German — provenance report

<!-- Generated from authored/german-basics.json by scripts/authored_decks.py. Do not edit: change the dossier and rebuild. -->

**Deck:** [`decks/german-basics.ttl`](../decks/german-basics.ttl) · **Cards:** 125 · **Licence:** [CC0 1.0 Universal](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/) · **Compiled by:** Anton Wiklund · **Created:** 2026-10-04

125 basic German words and phrases for beginners: the numbers 0–20, the tens and 100, the days of the week, the months, eight colours, family members, greetings and polite phrases, and everyday nouns, adjectives and verbs. The front shows the German word in current spelling; nouns, days and months are given with their definite article (der Tisch, die Tür, das Buch). The back gives its English and Swedish meaning, or the digits for a number, with the plural of most nouns in a note. Words, genders and meanings from Wikidata's lexemes and a public-domain US Government course and phrase book (the Foreign Service Institute's German Basic Course and the War Department's German Phrase Book), checked against German and English Wiktionary, Folkets lexikon and the official German spelling rules.

## Licensing

The deck is CC0 1.0. Its content comes from three sources whose terms allow any reuse: Wikidata's lexemes and items (CC0 1.0: German lemmas, genders, plurals, glosses, translations and German, English and Swedish labels), the Foreign Service Institute's German Basic Course (1961) and the War Department's German Phrase Book TM 30-606 (1943), both works of the United States Government with no copyright protection under 17 U.S.C. § 105 (the German greetings with their meaning, and a few facts of usage in the notes: Sonnabend in northern and eastern Germany, meine Frau, sein Sohn, Sie as the formal address). Section 105 applies in the United States; what the deck takes from these two works is the German form and English meaning of standard greetings and such facts of usage, which are not protectable expression anywhere, so the deck's CC0 dedication does not depend on § 105 applying outside the US. The phrase book's notice that it "is not to be republished … without the consent of the War Department" and its "RESTRICTED" marking are a wartime distribution instruction, not a copyright; what the deck takes from it is the gute Nacht card (a two-word greeting) and the facts in two notes, the gloss "see you again" for auf Wiedersehen and guten Tag as a daytime greeting; all three are uncopyrightable facts of usage, confirmed by the other sources. The selection of words is the authors' own. The English and Swedish renderings not taken from Wikidata are the usual equivalents chosen by the authors; several of them are the same short stock glosses that English Wiktionary, German Wiktionary or Folkets lexikon give, as the method says. Single words and fixed greetings such as "good night" or "god natt" are facts of usage, not protectable expression, so this does not carry those sources' licences into the deck; no definition, example, comment or list was taken from them. German Wiktionary (CC BY-SA 4.0), English Wiktionary (CC BY-SA 4.0), Folkets lexikon (CC BY-SA 2.5) and the Amtliches Regelwerk der deutschen Rechtschreibung (CC BY 4.0) were used for verification only: every fact in a note has a CC0 or public-domain content source (method, step 8), and the Regelwerk's spelling rules and German Wiktionary's regional labels only confirm them. So no source requires attribution or share-alike for the deck, although all are credited in its provenance. The quotations in this provenance report are not covered by the deck's CC0 dedication or the repository's MIT licence: quotations from German and English Wiktionary are © Wiktionary contributors, CC BY-SA 4.0; quotations from Folkets lexikon are CC BY-SA 2.5; quotations from the Amtliches Regelwerk are © 2024 Geschäftsstelle des Rats für deutsche Rechtschreibung, CC BY 4.0; quotations from the FSI course and the War Department phrase book are in the public domain.

## Method

1. Who did the work: Anton Wiklund compiled this deck with the help of AI agents (Claude, by Anthropic), which did the research, drafting and cross-checking at his direction. The cards were checked by machine (live Wikidata and the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators) and in independent review rounds by further Claude agents, each logged under Quality control with its findings and how they were resolved. Anton Wiklund reviews every deck in full before it is released.
2. Word list. A list of 125 words and phrases for a first German course was drawn up by hand from the library editor's brief (numbers 0–20, the tens and 100; days; months; colours; family; greetings and polite phrases; everyday nouns, adjectives and verbs), choosing the most basic, standard word for each concept and avoiding words whose everyday form differs by region (see Excluded). No frequency list, textbook word list or phrase-book list was copied: the public-domain US Government course and phrase book below were read only for the meaning of greetings already on the list and for facts in the notes.
3. Wikidata lexemes. SPARQL query 1 fetched every German lexeme (language Q188) whose lemma is a candidate, with its lexical category, grammatical gender (P5185), senses, English and German glosses and sense items (P5137). Phrases not found were looked up with the lexeme search (API calls 2): Wikidata has no German lexeme for guten Tag, guten Abend, gute Nacht or auf Wiedersehen. The full JSON of the lexeme chosen for each word (the numeral lexeme for numbers, the noun lexeme for nouns, the verb lexeme for verbs, and so on) was fetched with API calls 3; it gave the nominative plural form of each noun (the form with the features plural Q146786 and nominative Q131105). The English and Swedish lexemes named by the senses' translation statements (P5972) were fetched with API calls 4, and query 7 looked for English and Swedish senses that point to the German senses.
4. Wikidata items. The items linked from the senses (P5137) were fetched with API calls 5 (labels and aliases in German, English, Swedish and mul). For concepts whose lexeme sense has no item (the colours red, blue, white and brown; cold; the greetings guten Tag and guten Abend) items were found with the item search (API calls 6). The items give the English and Swedish labels for numbers, days, months, colours, family members and everyday things, and the German label or alias that the builder checks against the front.
5. Phrases. For the greetings with no lexeme, and as a second content source for the others, a public-domain US Government course and a phrase book on the Internet Archive were read (calls 9 and 10): the Foreign Service Institute's German Basic Course (1961), whose Unit 1 basic sentences give Guten Morgen, Guten Tag ("Hello (Good day)"), Guten Abend, Auf Wiedersehen ("good bye"), danke, bitte, ja and nein with their English meaning (its Unit 4 also gives the facts behind the notes on Sonnabend, meine Frau and the possessive sein); and the War Department's German Phrase Book TM 30-606 (1943), whose greetings page gives "Good night — Gute Nacht", the only source of that card's content. The FSI text was read in the Internet Archive's OCR text; the phrase book's OCR text is poor, so its pages 10–17 were rendered from the scanned PDF with PyMuPDF (call 10) and read directly.
6. Writing the cards. The front is the German word in the current (post-reform) spelling, as in the lexeme's lemma. Nouns, the days and the months are capitalised and preceded by the definite article that matches the lexeme's grammatical gender (der for masculine, die for feminine, das for neuter); every gender was confirmed against German Wiktionary's Genus. Numbers, colours and other adjectives, verbs (in the infinitive) and the interjections are in lower case, as in the dictionary. The multi-word greetings are given in their dictionary form, lower case except for the noun (guten Morgen, auf Wiedersehen), as Wikidata, German Wiktionary and the official word list write them. Entschuldigung, a noun used on its own as an apology, is capitalised and has no article; its note gives the noun. Of the two official spellings tschüss and tschüs, the card uses tschüss (the Wikidata and German Wiktionary lemma) and the note names tschüs.
7. The back is our own short English and Swedish rendering of the main sense: for nouns the bare noun, for verbs the infinitive (English "to …", Swedish "att …"), for numbers the digits, tagged zxx (text in no language). English and Swedish follow the Wikidata labels where an item exists and its label is the everyday word; otherwise they are the standard English and Swedish equivalents chosen by the authors and checked in English Wiktionary and Folkets lexikon (step 9). Where German has one word for two English or Swedish words, both are given (Stadt: town, city; Straße: street, road / gata, väg; groß: big, large; Großvater: farfar eller morfar). Swedish uses lower case for days and months. Every text is tagged with its language: the front de, the back en and sv, digits zxx.
8. Notes. A short note was added where it helps a beginner and the sources confirm it: the nominative plural of countable nouns (from the lexeme form, checked against German Wiktionary; not given for Wasser, Milch, Geld and Arbeit, whose plurals are rare or have another meaning), the spelling of sechzehn, sechzig, siebzehn, siebzig and dreißig, einhundert (a Wikidata alias of 100), Sonnabend (northern and eastern Germany) and Jänner (Austria), weiß as a form of wissen, Schwester also meaning nurse, Mann also husband, Frau also wife and Mrs, Strasse in Switzerland, groß also tall, Wie geht es Ihnen?, the possessive sein, guten Tag as a daytime greeting, “see you again” as another rendering of auf Wiedersehen, tschüss as a goodbye among friends and its spelling tschüs, the other uses of bitte, and the noun die Entschuldigung. Notes are our own wording, and each note's fact comes from a content source: Wikidata (the senses husband L7302-S3, wife L2945-S2 and nurse L34032-S4 with their items; Jänner's location of sense usage, Austria; the Swiss lemma Strasse of Straße; the lexemes tschüs and possessive sein; tschüss's gloss "freundschaftlicher Verabschiedungsgruß"), the FSI course (Sonnabend in northern and eastern Germany, meine Frau for one's wife, sein Sohn, Sie as the formal address, Frau Kunze, Wie geht es Ihnen?) or the War Department phrase book ("See you again — Auf Wiedersehen", "Good day or Good afternoon — Guten Tag"). German Wiktionary and the Regelwerk only confirm them. In review round 3 the notes on gute Nacht, tschüss, auf Wiedersehen and guten Tag, which had followed German Wiktionary's definitions, were rewritten or removed for this reason (see quality control, round 3).
9. Cross-checking. Every German word was looked up in German Wiktionary (calls 12: its wikitext, read with Python): spelling, part of speech, the gender of every noun against the card's article, the nominative plural, the first meaning, and its English and Swedish translations (the evidence quotes the first English and the first Swedish translation line of the entry; where those belong to a sense other than the card's, as for hallo and Straße, the evidence quotes the lines of the matching sense instead). Every English meaning was checked against the German section of English Wiktionary (calls 13). Every Swedish word was checked in Folkets lexikon (calls 14), one look-up per Swedish word on the card, English → Swedish, or Swedish → English when the first direction had no match; the look-up prefers an entry of the card's word class. The spelling points listed under the Rechtschreibrat source were checked in the official rules and word list of 2024 (call 11). A Python script built the evidence lines from the responses saved during authoring, so each quotation is what the source returned; wiki markup was rendered as plain text (links as their text, label templates such as {{K|…}} and {{ugs.}} as their names in brackets, gender markers dropped), and lists of translations longer than 140 characters were cut. The raw responses were working files and are not published; the code that read them (the Wiktionary parsing, the word-list look-up in the Regelwerk, the PDF text extraction and the Folkets matching) is recorded under queries 11, 12 and 14.
10. Duden and DWDS. The brief asked for each German form to be verified in Duden online or the DWDS. The DWDS terms of use (https://www.dwds.de/d/nutzungsbedingungen) say: "Jegliche Nutzung der Inhalte des DWDS, einschließlich jedoch nicht beschränkt auf automatisierte Abfragen und Auswertungen (Crawlen, Parsen, Text- und Data-Mining), sofern nicht über § 60d UrhG zulässig, ist nur mit ausdrücklicher Genehmigung gestattet." An AI agent can only consult a dictionary through automated requests, so the DWDS was not used: one entry page (https://www.dwds.de/wb/Tisch) had been fetched before the terms were read, and nothing from it is in this deck or its evidence. Duden online was not consulted either. German Wiktionary (open licence, automated access allowed) and the official spelling rules of the Rat für deutsche Rechtschreibung took their place as verification sources.
11. Machine checks. The dossier's Wikidata checks (270 checks on 108 items: the German label or alias of each linked item that matches the front, its English and Swedish label or alias that matches the back, the mul digit label of each number, and, since review round 3, the labels of the items behind the notes on Mann, Frau, Schwester, Januar, Straße and auf Wiedersehen: husband, wife, nurse, Austria, the Swiss Standard German label Strasse, goodbye and adjö) are re-run against live Wikidata by the builder on every build. Where an item's label does not match the card, no check was added and the difference is listed under quality control, round 0. Wikidata lexemes cannot be checked by the builder (it checks items only); the lexeme facts in the evidence were read from the API responses of 4 October 2026.
12. Excluded: words whose everyday form differs by region (Brötchen/Semmel, Junge/Bub, Sonnabend and Jänner, which appear only in notes), words with two equally common meanings that a single card cannot separate (Morgen/morgen: morning/tomorrow; die Bank: bench/bank), pairs a beginner cannot tell apart without context (wissen/kennen, both "to know"), the pronouns du/Sie, which need more than a flashcard, the colloquial Mama, Papa, Oma and Opa, and the colours orange, rosa and lila, which do not inflect like the others.

## Selection

125 cards: the cardinal numbers 0–20, the tens 30–90 and 100 (29); the seven days of the week; the twelve months; eight colours (red, blue, green, yellow, black, white, grey, brown); eight family members (mother, father, brother, sister, son, daughter, grandfather, grandmother); twelve greetings and polite phrases (hallo, guten Morgen, guten Tag, guten Abend, gute Nacht, tschüss, auf Wiedersehen, danke, bitte, Entschuldigung, ja, nein); 25 everyday nouns (Haus, Wasser, Brot, Milch, Apfel, Buch, Tisch, Stuhl, Tür, Fenster, Hund, Katze, Stadt, Straße, Schule, Mann, Frau, Kind, Geld, Arbeit, Hand, Tag, Nacht, Jahr, Woche); eight adjectives (groß, klein, gut, schlecht, neu, alt, kalt, warm); and 16 common verbs in the infinitive (sein, haben, gehen, kommen, machen, sprechen, essen, trinken, wohnen, lesen, schreiben, schlafen, arbeiten, kaufen, sehen, sagen). The list was chosen by the deck's authors for a first course, not copied from any frequency list, textbook or phrase book. Every word has a Wikidata lexeme except guten Tag, guten Abend, gute Nacht and auf Wiedersehen, which come from the public-domain FSI course and the War Department's phrase book (guten Tag and guten Abend also from Wikidata items). The standard form common to Germany, Austria and Switzerland was chosen where one exists; where usage differs by country or region, the card gives the form standard in Germany and the note names the variant (Sonnabend, Jänner, Strasse). Left out: regional words (Brötchen/Semmel, Junge/Bub), words with two equally common meanings (Morgen, Bank), word pairs a beginner cannot tell apart on one card (wissen/kennen), the pronouns du and Sie, colloquial family words (Mama, Papa, Oma, Opa) and the uninflected colours orange, rosa and lila. The deck is studied front to back only: although no two backs are identical, the reverse direction would be ambiguous for the greetings (hello: hallo or guten Tag; bye and goodbye: tschüss or auf Wiedersehen, both hej då in Swedish).

## Queries

**1. German lexemes (Q188) for every candidate lemma, with lexical category, grammatical gender (P5185), senses, English and German glosses and the item for each sense (P5137). POST to https://query.wikidata.org/sparql** (Wikidata (German lexemes and items))

```
SELECT ?lexeme ?lemma ?category ?gender ?sense ?glossEn ?glossDe ?item WHERE {
  VALUES ?lemma { "null"@de "eins"@de "zwei"@de "drei"@de "vier"@de "fünf"@de "sechs"@de "sieben"@de "acht"@de "neun"@de "zehn"@de "elf"@de "zwölf"@de "dreizehn"@de "vierzehn"@de "fünfzehn"@de "sechzehn"@de "siebzehn"@de "achtzehn"@de "neunzehn"@de "zwanzig"@de "dreißig"@de "vierzig"@de "fünfzig"@de "sechzig"@de "siebzig"@de "achtzig"@de "neunzig"@de "hundert"@de "Montag"@de "Dienstag"@de "Mittwoch"@de "Donnerstag"@de "Freitag"@de "Samstag"@de "Sonntag"@de "Januar"@de "Februar"@de "März"@de "April"@de "Mai"@de "Juni"@de "Juli"@de "August"@de "September"@de "Oktober"@de "November"@de "Dezember"@de "rot"@de "blau"@de "grün"@de "gelb"@de "schwarz"@de "weiß"@de "grau"@de "braun"@de "Mutter"@de "Vater"@de "Bruder"@de "Schwester"@de "Sohn"@de "Tochter"@de "Großvater"@de "Großmutter"@de "hallo"@de "guten Morgen"@de "guten Tag"@de "guten Abend"@de "gute Nacht"@de "tschüss"@de "auf Wiedersehen"@de "danke"@de "bitte"@de "Entschuldigung"@de "ja"@de "nein"@de "Haus"@de "Wasser"@de "Brot"@de "Milch"@de "Apfel"@de "Buch"@de "Tisch"@de "Stuhl"@de "Tür"@de "Fenster"@de "Hund"@de "Katze"@de "Stadt"@de "Straße"@de "Schule"@de "Mann"@de "Frau"@de "Kind"@de "Geld"@de "Arbeit"@de "Hand"@de "Tag"@de "Nacht"@de "Jahr"@de "Woche"@de "groß"@de "klein"@de "gut"@de "schlecht"@de "neu"@de "alt"@de "kalt"@de "warm"@de "sein"@de "haben"@de "gehen"@de "kommen"@de "machen"@de "sprechen"@de "essen"@de "trinken"@de "wohnen"@de "lesen"@de "schreiben"@de "schlafen"@de "arbeiten"@de "kaufen"@de "sehen"@de "sagen"@de "tschüs"@de "Guten Morgen"@de "Guten Tag"@de "Guten Abend"@de "Gute Nacht"@de "Auf Wiedersehen"@de "Sonnabend"@de }
  ?lexeme dct:language wd:Q188 ;
          wikibase:lemma ?lemma ;
          wikibase:lexicalCategory ?category .
  OPTIONAL { ?lexeme wdt:P5185 ?gender . }
  OPTIONAL {
    ?lexeme ontolex:sense ?sense .
    OPTIONAL { ?sense skos:definition ?glossEn . FILTER(LANG(?glossEn) = "en") }
    OPTIONAL { ?sense skos:definition ?glossDe . FILTER(LANG(?glossDe) = "de") }
    OPTIONAL { ?sense wdt:P5137 ?item . }
  }
}
```

**11. The official German spelling rules and word list (2024): the Rechtschreibrat's page, the PDF, its text (PyMuPDF) and the look-ups of the words checked** (Amtliches Regelwerk der deutschen Rechtschreibung: Regeln und Wörterverzeichnis (2024))

```
curl -sL -A "solid-memo deck research (https://github.com/antwika/solid-memo)" "https://www.rechtschreibrat.com/regeln-und-woerterverzeichnis/"
curl -sL -A "solid-memo deck research (https://github.com/antwika/solid-memo)" "https://www.rechtschreibrat.com/DOX/RfdR_Amtliches-Regelwerk_2024.pdf"
uv run --with pymupdf python3 pdftext.py regelwerk-2024.pdf regelwerk-2024.txt   # page.get_text() for every page
python3 rat2.py "dreißig" "weiß" "groß:" "Straße" "tschüs" "Wiedersehen" "hallo" "danke" "bitte:" "Tür" "sechzehn" "siebzehn" "siebzig" "sechzig" "Großmutter" "Großvater" "Fenster" "null" "hundert"   # word-list lines starting with the word, from the page headed "Wörterverzeichnis a/A" on
grep -n -E "^§ ?25|§ 25|Maß, Straße|Straße" regelwerk-2024.txt; sed -n '1670,1715p' regelwerk-2024.txt
# pdftext.py:
doc = pymupdf.open(sys.argv[1])
for i, p in enumerate(doc): out.write(f"\n=====PAGE {i+1}=====\n" + p.get_text())
# rat2.py (word-list look-up):
lines = open("regelwerk-2024.txt").read().split("\n")
start = next(i for i, l in enumerate(lines) if re.match(r"^Wörterverzeichnis\s+a/A", l))
page = (PDF page number from the last "=====PAGE n=====" marker, printed page number from the line after it)
for each line from start - 3 on and each word w: if re.match(r"^" + w + r"\b", line): print(page, the line and the next two)
```

```
# index (Python):
for w in ET.parse(fn).getroot().iter("word"):
    head = w.get("value").replace("|", "")
    idx.setdefault(head.lower(), []).append(("word", head, w.get("class"), [t.get("value") for t in w.findall("translation")]))
    for idm in w.findall("idiom"):
        idx.setdefault(idm.get("value").lower().rstrip("!.").strip(), []).append(("idiom", head, None, [t.get("value") for t in idm.findall("translation")]))
# for each Swedish word on the card: entries of any English word on the card ("to" removed; also bye-bye for tschüss, good day for guten Tag, excuse for Entschuldigung)
# whose translations include it (ignoring case and a final "!" or "."), or Swedish entries whose translations include the English;
# best = same word class as the card first, then most matches, then earliest match in the entry
```

## Quality control

7 rounds, 41 findings: 22 fixed, 2 rejected after checking, 17 needing no change. Every card's Wikidata checks (270 in all) are re-run against live Wikidata by `scripts/authored_decks.py check` before every build.

### Round 0: Sources, licences and machine checks (2026-10-04)

**Reviewer:** Claude (AI) — authoring agent, machine checks · **Scope:** All 125 cards: every German form, article, plural, English and Swedish meaning and note against the content sources and the verification sources; the builder's Wikidata checks.

Every card has evidence from a content source (Wikidata, the FSI course or the War Department phrase book) and from German and English Wiktionary; every Swedish back is also checked in Folkets lexikon. German Wiktionary agrees with the spelling, part of speech and article of every card, and with the plural of every noun that has a plural note. The builder's Wikidata checks cover the German, English, Swedish or mul labels and aliases of 104 linked items (253 checks); they all pass. Discrepancies between the sources and how they were resolved are listed below.

| Card | Issue | Resolution | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| null, zwei, drei, vier, fuenf, sechs, sieben, acht, neun | The number items label the number as a noun: de labels "Null", "Zwei", "Drei", "Vier", "Fünf", "Acht"; Q23488 (6), Q23350 (7) and Q19108 (9) have no de label and only capitalised aliases (Sechs, Sieben, Neun). | The cards keep the lower-case numeral, the lemma of the numeral lexemes and of German Wiktionary; no German label check for these nine items. The mul digit label is checked for every number, and the de alias where it is the lower-case numeral (eins, zehn to hundert). | no change needed |
| rot, blau, weiss, braun | The colour items Q3142, Q1088, Q23444 and Q47071 have the capitalised noun as de label (Rot, Blau, Weiß, Braun) and no lower-case alias. | The cards keep the adjective (rot, blau, weiß, braun), the lemma of the adjective lexemes; English and Swedish labels are checked, German is not for these four. | no change needed |
| weiss | The adjective lexeme L732372 (weiß) has no senses. | The meaning comes from the item Q23444 (en white, sv vit), confirmed by German and English Wiktionary and Folkets. | no change needed |
| grossvater, grossmutter | Wikidata's Swedish labels for grandfather and grandmother (Q9238344, Q9235758) are the descriptive "förälders far" and "förälders mor"; Swedish has no single neutral word. | The cards give "farfar eller morfar" and "farmor eller mormor", as Folkets lexikon and German Wiktionary translate them. No Swedish label check. | no change needed |

| guten-abend, neu | The items Q19279366 (guten Abend) and Q15650394 (neu) have no Swedish label. | Swedish checked in Folkets (good evening → god kväll; new → ny). | no change needed |

### Round 1: Factual accuracy (2026-10-04)

**Reviewer:** Claude (AI) — independent Factual accuracy reviewer · **Scope:** All 125 cards: German spelling, articles, plurals, English and Swedish meanings and notes, against the official Regelwerk 2024, German Wiktionary and a live run of the builder's Wikidata checks.

No card was found factually wrong; all 253 Wikidata checks passed. Two warnings: the front "sein" can also be the possessive "his/its", and the selection overstated that only words common to Germany, Austria and Switzerland were kept. Three suggestions: Liechtenstein in the Strasse note, the phrase book called a "course", and the vowel length behind tschüs/tschüss. Each finding was checked against the sources; the two warnings and the course wording were fixed, the other two suggestions declined.

| Card | Issue | Resolution | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| sein | The front "sein" has two right answers: the verb "to be" and the possessive "his/its" (German Wiktionary has a Possessivpronomen section); the card had no note. | Confirmed in German Wiktionary (sections Verb/Hilfsverb and Possessivpronomen) and in Wikidata, which has a separate possessive lexeme L411090 (gloss "his"). Added the frontNote "verb" / "verb" and the backNote "Also the possessive sein, “his”: sein Sohn." / "Även possessivt sein, ”hans”: sein Sohn.", with Wikidata L411090 and FSI Unit 4 ("His son … Sein Sohn ist Vizekonsul in München") as content sources and German Wiktionary's Possessivpronomen section as verification. The note gives only "his", the sense the CC0 and public-domain sources state. | fixed |
| deck | The selection says only standard German used in Germany, Austria and Switzerland alike was kept, but the notes on Januar (Jänner in Austria), Straße (Strasse in Switzerland) and Samstag (Sonnabend) show otherwise. | Agreed. The selection now says: "The standard form common to Germany, Austria and Switzerland was chosen where one exists; where usage differs by country or region, the card gives the form standard in Germany and the note names the variant (Sonnabend, Jänner, Strasse)." | fixed |
| strasse | The note "In Switzerland written Strasse" leaves out Liechtenstein; the official rule (§ 25 E2) covers both and is permissive ("kann"). | Declined. The note's content source is now Wikidata's Swiss Standard German (de-ch) lemma "Strasse" of L44061 (and the de-ch label of Q79007, a new machine check); no CC0 or public-domain source gives Liechtenstein, and the Regelwerk is a verification source only. Swiss usage, which the note describes, does write ss throughout; the Regelwerk's E2 quote stays in the evidence. | rejected |
| deck | The description (en and sv) calls the FSI course and the War Department's phrase book "two public-domain US Government courses"; TM 30-606 is a phrase book. | Fixed in the description ("a public-domain US Government course and phrase book" / "en amerikansk statlig kurs och parlör fria från upphovsrätt") and in method steps 2 and 5. The selection now says "the War Department's phrase book". | fixed |
| tschuess | The note "Also spelt tschüs" hides that the official word list ties each spelling to a vowel length (tschüs long, tschüss short). | Declined: the vowel length is given only by the Regelwerk, a verification source; the spelling tschüs itself now has a CC0 content source (Wikidata lexeme L584956, lemma "tschüs"). The note was reworded for round 3 ("A goodbye among friends. Also spelt tschüs."). | rejected |

### Round 2: Language, translation and language tags (2026-10-04)

**Reviewer:** Claude (AI) — independent Language, translation and language tags reviewer · **Scope:** All 125 cards: language tags of every text, German spelling and grammar, English and Swedish idiom, the study direction, and the description.

No errors or warnings: every text is tagged (de fronts, zxx digits, en and sv backs and notes), the German follows current spelling, and the English and Swedish are idiomatic. Three suggestions: the phrase book called a "course" and an ambiguous front-side sentence in the description, the dated Swedish "Hur mår ni?" in the gehen note, and Swedish syster also meaning nurse. All three were applied, the last in a form that has a CC0 source.

| Card | Issue | Resolution | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| deck | The description calls the War Department's German Phrase Book a "course", and its sentence "The front shows the German word in current spelling, nouns, days and months with their definite article" (and the Swedish one) reads as if nouns, days and months were further things on the front. | Fixed in both languages: "… a public-domain US Government course and phrase book …" and "The front shows the German word in current spelling; nouns, days and months are given with their definite article (der Tisch, die Tür, das Buch). The back gives …" / "… en amerikansk statlig kurs och parlör …" and "Framsidan visar det tyska ordet i nutida stavning; substantiv, veckodagar och månader står med bestämd artikel (…). Baksidan ger …". | fixed |
| gehen | The Swedish note renders the formal Wie geht es Ihnen? as "Hur mår ni?"; since the du reform Swedish ni as a polite singular reads dated, and learners may take it as the counterpart of Sie. | Agreed. The note is now "Also in Wie geht es Ihnen? “How are you?” (polite Sie form)." / "Även i Wie geht es Ihnen? ”Hur mår du?” (artigt tilltal med Sie)." The polite-form fact has a public-domain content source, FSI Unit 11 ("Sie indicates a formal relationship between the speaker and the person or persons addressed"), added to the evidence. | fixed |
| schwester | The Swedish note could point out that Swedish syster also means nurse (sjuksyster), a memory aid for Swedish learners. | Applied in a sourced form: no CC0 source gives syster alone as nurse (the Swedish lexeme L32409 has only the kinship sense, and SAOL could not be read as text), but Wikidata's nurse item Q186360 has the Swedish alias "sjuksyster". The Swedish note is now "Plural: die Schwestern. Även sjuksköterska (kortform av Krankenschwester; jfr svenska sjuksyster).", with Q186360 in the evidence and a machine check of the alias. | fixed |

### Round 3: Licensing, attribution and documentation (2026-10-04)

**Reviewer:** Claude (AI) — independent Licensing, attribution and documentation reviewer · **Scope:** The licences and licence evidence of all seven sources, the deck's attribution, the method and queries, and the evidence of about 28 cards against live sources.

All seven licences and the attribution in the built deck were confirmed. The findings were in the notes and the documentation: one note closely followed a CC BY-SA definition and several note facts were supported only by verification sources; one locator was wrong; the phrase book was called a course; helper scripts were not recorded; two Wiktionary quotes came from the wrong sense; and the US-only scope of 17 U.S.C. § 105 was not addressed. Every finding was checked and fixed. Every note fact now has a CC0 or public-domain content source (Wikidata lexemes and items, the FSI course, the War Department phrase book), found by fetching the Wikidata entities again (query 15) and searching the FSI text (query 16); notes with no such source were rewritten or removed.
